newsitem.title: USA: Motorola plans satellite system - WSJ.
newsitem.headline: Motorola plans satellite system - WSJ.

text.p: Motorola Inc, looking to raise its profile in the satellite-systems business, is planning to launch a $12.9 billion network that would deliver high-speed data and video to businesses, broadcasters and telecommunications companies, the Wall Street Journal said.

In Tuesday's electronic edition, the Journal said the venture poses a direct challenge to wireless pioneer Craig McCaw and his Teledesic Corp, a proposed $9 billion high-speed satellite system that has attracted such investors as Microsoft Corp Chairman Bill Gates.
Motorola's plans were disclosed in documents filed with federal regulators.
John Pientka, vice president and general manager of Motorola's advanced systems division, said the company is not aiming to put McCaw out of business.
"There's a lot of room in the satellite business," Pientka said. "It's entering a whole new phase."
"This is about Motorola trying to wreck Teledesic because they hate the idea of Boeing competing as a satellite provider," Teledesic President Russell Daggett said.
Motorola, which has been a key equipment supplier for other business of McCaw, recently lost out to Boeing Co in bidding to build the 288-satellite Teledesic network.
"This is about monopoly profits for Motorola producing satellites," Daggett said.
But Pientka said, "We think competition grows the market."
Motorola's system is called Celestri. It is the third major low-orbit system for Motorola, and would deliver data to the ground at variable rates, between 64,000 and 155 million bits per second.
Motorola plans to file for Celestri with the Federal Communications Commission on Friday. It would seek in part to use the same portion of the radio-frequency spectrum that Teledesic plans to use.

Teledesic, which is planning to begin service in 2002, had planned to give Motorola major contracts for portions of its payload even though it chose Boeing as its prime contractor, Teledesic Chief Executive David Twyver said.
Since the Celestri filing, Motorola's chances of receiving that contract "are negative," Twyver said.
